column2: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is issuing the first federal fuel-economy rule for light trucks, vans, and jeep-type four-wheel-drive vehicles (called 'nonpassenger automobiles') rated at 6,000 pounds gross vehicle weight or less, for model year 1979 only. Manufacturers must achieve a production-weighted fleet average of 17.2 miles per gallon, or may elect a split standard of 17.2 mpg for other nonpassenger automobiles plus 15.8 mpg for jeep-type vehicles, with a $5 penalty per 0.1 mpg shortfall per vehicle. The rule directly affects domestic manufacturers — General Motors, Ford, Chrysler, American Motors, and International Harvester — plus captive imports (foreign-built pickups like the Chevrolet LUV and Ford Courier sold by domestic firms). NHTSA considered but rejected taking no action, extending the standard to trucks over 6,000 pounds (data not available), and setting higher or lower levels, ultimately lowering its proposed 18.7 mpg to 17.2 mpg to reflect an 8 percent fuel-economy loss from revised EPA test procedures. The primary environmental benefit is roughly 102.5 million gallons of gasoline saved annually (about 0.07-0.1 percent of 1975 U.S. consumption), with minor secondary effects from increased use of aluminum, plastics, and catalytic-converter metals. Every affected manufacturer objected that the proposed level was too high given 1979 emission and test-procedure changes, and no consumer or public-interest groups submitted substantive comments.

column2: NHTSA is setting the first federal fuel-economy standard for model year 1979 'nonpassenger automobiles' — pickup trucks, vans, and jeep-type four-wheel-drive vehicles rated at 6,000 pounds gross vehicle weight or less — as required by section 502(b) of Title V of the Motor Vehicle Information and Cost Savings Act. The final rule sets 17.2 mpg for the general class and 15.8 mpg for jeep-type vehicles (four-wheel drive, off-highway capable, wheelbase not more than 110 inches), with manufacturers allowed to include their jeep-type vehicles in the general 17.2 mpg fleet at their option. Compliance is measured as a production-weighted average across each manufacturer's fleet, and the proposed level of 18.7 mpg was lowered by 8 percent to reflect measured effects of revised EPA test procedures.

column2: The rule directly affects U.S. light-truck manufacturers — General Motors, Ford, Chrysler, American Motors Corporation, and International Harvester — because domestic nonpassenger automobiles average much lower fuel economy than imports (15.9 mpg for all domestics compared with 22.1 mpg for imports in MY 1976). Total MY 1979 domestic production was projected at about 1 million vehicles (52.6% GM, 27.9% Ford, 16.3% Chrysler, 3.7% AMC), plus about 100,000 'captive imports' — foreign-built pickups such as the Chevrolet LUV (built by Isuzu) and Ford Courier (built by Toyo-Kogyo) sold by domestic firms. Consumers, the United Auto Workers, and the U.S. Forest Service also weighed in, the Forest Service concerned that design constraints would push truck buyers toward heavier, costlier vehicles.

column2: NHTSA considered four principal alternatives: taking no action (rejected because the statute requires a standard); extending the standard to nonpassenger automobiles between 6,000 and 10,000 pounds gross vehicle weight (rejected because EPA baseline fuel-economy data for heavier trucks were not yet available); setting standards for model years beyond 1979 (deferred to future rulemakings because of uncertainty about market shifts to unregulated heavier vehicles); and setting a higher or lower level (a higher level was rejected because it could push consumers or manufacturers into the unregulated over-6,000-pound class, and a lower level was rejected as inconsistent with the Act's 'maximum feasible average fuel economy' requirement). The agency also considered whether to treat all nonpassenger automobiles as one class or split them, ultimately creating two classes with a separate 15.8 mpg level for jeep-type vehicles, and chose to include captive imports in domestic manufacturers' fleets for MY 1979 only.

column2: The main environmental benefit is gasoline savings: about 102.5 million gallons annually versus 1976 levels (roughly 0.07-0.1 percent of the 10.2 billion gallons the U.S. consumed in 1975), or 691 million to 1.027 billion gallons over the fleet's 10-year lifetime, equivalent to 18.13 to 26.9 million barrels of oil. Vehicle redesign is expected to reduce cast iron and steel use by about 42 million pounds while adding roughly 5.26 million pounds each of aluminum and plastics as substitutes, plus about 2,200 troy ounces more platinum and palladium for larger catalytic converters — a 9 percent (not 13.7 percent, as initially estimated) increase for nonpassenger automobiles under 6,000 pounds. Secondary effects on water quality, industrial water demand, stationary-source air pollution, solid waste (because plastics resist landfill decomposition), and community noise are all characterized as minor. NHTSA concluded manufacturers had not shown a fuel-economy penalty from EPA's tighter MY 1979 NOx (nitrogen oxide) standard (lowered from 3.1 to 2.3 grams per mile), but accepted an 8 percent measured penalty from EPA's revised road-load test procedure (roughly a 30 percent increase in road-load horsepower setting).

column2: Sixteen commenters weighed in, dominated by manufacturers — American Motors, Chrysler, Ford, General Motors, and International Harvester — plus the UAW, several federal agencies (EPA, FEA, Interior, Labor, Agriculture, Forest Service, offices within DOT), the Society of the Plastics Industry, Consumers Union, and the University of Michigan; NHTSA specifically noted that 'no comments were received from consumer groups, or other public interest organizations' with substantive input. Virtually all manufacturers argued the proposed 18.7 mpg was too high, primarily because of expected fuel-economy penalties from the MY 1979 emission standard and test-procedure changes, with penalty estimates ranging from 3 percent (Ford, emissions only) to 10-15 percent (International Harvester); several urged separate, lower treatment for four-wheel-drive jeep-type vehicles, which led NHTSA to add the two-class option. Ford also challenged NHTSA's cost-benefit analysis, arguing compliance costs would be at least $100 per vehicle rather than NHTSA's $12 manufacturer / $24 retail estimate, and AMC argued its Jeep CJ vehicle was not an 'automobile' under Title V and opposed including captive imports as discriminatory toward non-importers.
